Description: The parent operation representing one full agent run, under which individual LLM calls and tool calls are nested as child spans.
The sequence of sub-steps or sub-goals the agent decided to pursue to fulfill the request, when the agent explicitly plans before acting.
Which conditional path or route the orchestration logic chose (e.g. which specialized workflow was selected for this request).
A unique ID for an entire task or journey, used to group all its individual steps together, or to add a new step to an existing task.
Records exactly where a step falls in the overall sequence and hierarchy of events, so everything displays in the correct order.
Identifies which conversation or user session a group of related tasks belongs to, so they can all be viewed together.
Whether the interaction occurred in dev, UAT, or production.
The name of the deploying application or microservice that hosts the agent.
The cluster and namespace the workload ran in.
The specific running instance that handled the request, useful for correlating with infrastructure-level logs/metrics.
Pass/fail outcome when a conversation or prompt is replayed against a test dataset before a release.
The interface or product surface the request came from (e.g. web chat, mobile app, Teams, IVR, internal portal).
Language the input was written/spoken in, if language detection is performed.
A record that the system fell back to a secondary model, cached response, or degraded behavior after a primary failure.
Records which AI company or service handled the request, such as OpenAI or Anthropic.
The name of the specific AI model asked to handle the request, such as GPT-4 or Claude.
The name of the AI model that actually generated the response, which can occasionally differ slightly from the one requested.
A setting that controls how creative or random the AI's answers are; higher values tend to produce more varied responses.
The list of messages sent into the AI as part of a conversation, tracked using this particular naming convention. Input message can be either from Human, System, Tool or another agent
The list of messages the AI sent back as its response, tracked using this particular naming convention.
The 'thinking' output of the model
Any specific strings configured to make the model stop generating early.
Why the model stopped generating — it completed naturally, hit a length limit, was cut off by a stop sequence, or triggered a tool call.
Source documents or passages the model's answer explicitly points to as support for its claims.
For streaming responses, the delay between the request and the first token being returned — a key user-experience metric.
Where the model itself is served from (e.g. vLLM/KServe endpoint, external API), distinct from the model name.
A message sent by the person using the AI, such as a question they typed in.
The specific inputs or values that were passed into a tool when the AI decided to use it.
A message containing the result of an external tool the AI used, such as the answer from a calculator or a search.
Version number of the tool
Unique identifier correlating a tool call with its corresponding result, especially when several tools are called in one turn.
The parameters/arguments the agent passed into the tool when invoking it.
The data or response the tool returned to the agent after execution.
How long the external tool took to execute and return.
Whether the tool call succeeded, failed, or timed out.
The actual text of one specific document that was found during a search or lookup, such as a knowledge-base search.
The search query issued against the knowledge base or vector store or inbuilt memory to fetch relevant context.
The set of documents/passages returned by the retrieval step, along with their relevance scores.
Which document repository or vector index the content was retrieved from.
The bank's internal data classification level applied to this interaction (e.g. public, internal, confidential, restricted).
Time taken to complete the retrieval/search step.
The parameters sent to, and data returned from, an MCP tool call.
A score from an automated Guardrail evaluator (being called from the source) or rule assessing response quality, correctness, or relevance
Complete information of guardrail including input/output, version, guardrail name and ID
Which specific quality dimension was being scored (e.g. helpfulness, factual accuracy, tone compliance).
A pointer to which OPA/Kuadrant policy evaluation applied to this boundary crossing and its allow/deny result — the audit trail for governance enforcement, not the enforcement itself.
The result of any toxicity, jailbreak, or policy-violation classifier run against user input or model output.
Whether sensitive personal or financial data was detected in the input or output, and what category it fell into.
The name/identity of the specific agent handling this task, relevant when multiple specialized agents exist (e.g. a routing agent vs. a fulfillment agent).
Version ID of the Agent
Which underlying framework built and runs the agent (e.g. LangGraph, Dify, Google ADK), useful when comparing behavior across frameworks.
Memory information which the agent retrieved from both short and long term memory bank
Thumbs up/down or star rating the end user gave the response, if the interface collects it.
A label or correction applied by a human reviewer during offline review or dataset curation.
Counts how much text, measured in small chunks called tokens, was sent to the AI as input. This is often used to estimate cost, since providers typically charge by token count.
Counts how much text the AI generated in its response, measured in tokens, which also affects cost.
The combined total of input and output tokens used for the request, giving a full picture of how much text was processed.
Some AI models do internal 'thinking' before giving a final answer, and this counts how much of that hidden reasoning was used, which can add to cost.
Captures the original question or instruction given to the AI, pulled from the detailed record of what happened during the request.
Captures the AI's response, pulled from the detailed record of what happened during the request.

A behind-the-scenes instruction given to the AI at the start of a conversation that sets its behavior or role, like telling it to act as a helpful assistant. It's usually invisible to the end user but shapes how the AI responds.
The standing instructions given to the model that shape its behavior for this use case, separate from the user's own message.
How long the model took to respond, and how long the end-to-end agent turn took overall.
The list of external tools or functions that were available for the AI to choose from during the request.
Records the name of an external tool the AI used, like a calculator, and marks the step as a 'tool' action.
Instances where the agent detected a failure or low-confidence result and re-attempted a step.
Lets you give the particular run a clear, custom name instead of a default technical one, so it's easier to recognize later.
Labels what kind of action happened, such as an AI model call, a chain of steps, or a tool being used, so it's easier to understand what occurred.
A unique ID for one specific step within a task, like a serial number, so that step can be found or linked to later. A run ID is parent to trace ID and each run ID can have multiple traces
Shows which earlier step a new step belongs under, which is how LangSmith builds its tree-like view of related steps.
Describes what kind of AI task was performed, like having a conversation or converting text into a numerical representation, so LangSmith can label it correctly.
Date and time the interaction, or each step within it, occurred.
Which internal agent or service initiated the cross-boundary call, used for gateway-layer policy enforcement and audit.
Records that something went wrong during the step, marking it as an error and saving details about what caused the problem.
The category and description of any failure that occurred anywhere in the agent's execution (LLM call, tool call, orchestration logic).
A marker on the specific span where the failure occurred, distinguishing it from spans that completed successfully.
The technical trace of where in the code the failure originated, used by engineering for debugging.
A record that a response was withheld or altered because it failed a safety or compliance check.
A record that the interaction was routed to a human reviewer/approver instead of being auto-resolved by the agent.
For stateful approval workflows, a reference to the approval record the policy engine checked against (who approved, when) — a compliance audit trail, not the raw decision engine.
Whether the input was text, voice (transcribed), image, or file upload.
Reference to any document, image, or file the user attached to the request (not the file itself, typically a pointer/ID).
Username or the agent who is triggering the action
